title: 'Dil Chahta Hai' at 25: The Film Nobody Wanted to Make That Changed Hindi Cinema
excerpt: Farhan Akhtar's directorial debut turned 25 in August 2026 with a cast reunion and the launch of Excel Origins, a new initiative to find the next generation of filmmakers.
body:
• Farhan Akhtar's directorial debut 'Dil Chahta Hai' turned 25 in August 2026, with the original cast reuniting for a celebration in Mumbai.
  • Akhtar revealed he waited eight months to get Aamir Khan to hear the script, refusing to use his father Javed Akhtar's connections for an introduction.
  • Excel Entertainment, the production house Akhtar co-founded with Ritesh Sidhwani for the film, has launched Excel Origins to discover and back new filmmakers.
  • The film is widely credited with redefining how friendship, urban youth, and modern relationships were portrayed in Hindi cinema.

Twenty-five years ago, a 26-year-old first-time director walked into a Bollywood industry obsessed with love triangles and told a story about three friends hanging out. Nobody wanted to make it. In August 2026, the cast and crew of 'Dil Chahta Hai' gathered in Mumbai to celebrate the film's silver jubilee — and to acknowledge that the movie had outlasted nearly every romantic drama released that year.

Farhan Akhtar's 2001 directorial debut, starring Aamir Khan, Saif Ali Khan, and Akshaye Khanna, with Preity Zinta, Sonali Kulkarni, and Dimple Kapadia in pivotal roles, didn't just change Hindi cinema's visual grammar. It gave an entire generation of urban Indians — and the diaspora scattered across the world — a vocabulary for what male friendship could look like on screen: unglamorous, unsentimental, and entirely real.

The Struggle to Get Made

In a recent interview with The Juggernaut, Akhtar revealed just how difficult the journey to production had been. "Casting Aamir Khan wasn't an easy task. Everyone said, 'I don't want to do a multi-hero film.' At the time, everyone wanted to do a love triangle," he recalled.

Akhtar spent eight months trying to get Khan to hear the complete script. Despite his father Javed Akhtar having co-written 'Lagaan' with Khan around the same period, Farhan deliberately avoided leveraging that connection. "I didn't ask for any special introduction. I kept knocking on doors and waited eight months before Aamir agreed to hear the full script," he said.

When Khan finally sat down to listen, the narration took an unexpected turn. According to Bollywood Hungama, Khan asked for a 15-minute power nap after hearing the first half — and slept for eight hours at Akhtar's home. The original script, Khan has since revealed, was written entirely in English, and he was initially worried the Hindi version would make him cringe. It didn't.

"Can't believe it's been 25 years. Akash, Sameer and Sid don't look like they've aged a day! Heart filled with gratitude to you, the audience, for keeping it alive and still relevant."

— Farhan Akhtar, via X

A Film That Rewrote the Rules

Released on August 10, 2001, 'Dil Chahta Hai' confounded audiences initially. There was no dramatic conflict in the first half, no villain, no songs that interrupted the narrative. Word of mouth drove its success, as Akhtar told Variety India: "For the longest time, people were wondering, 'yeh kahani jaa kahan rahi hai' (where is this story going?). We were so conditioned to some kind of a hook. It took a while for people to settle into that experience."

Saif Ali Khan, speaking at the anniversary reunion, credited the production with changing how Hindi films were made. The crew, which included Zoya Akhtar as an assistant director, estimated a 105-day shoot after reading the script and wrapped on exactly the 105th day. "They changed the culture of how films are made," Khan said.

He also recalled a detail that stuck with him: after shooting on a Goa beach, the crew asked everyone to pick up litter before leaving. "Let's leave the beach cleaner than we found it," they said.

Goa, Tara, and the Slap That Took 17 Takes

Two elements of the film have become cultural landmarks. Goa's Chapora Fort, where the three leads sat against the backdrop of the sea, is now commonly referred to as the "Dil Chahta Hai Fort" — a touchstone for friend groups who recreate the moment. And Dimple Kapadia as the enigmatic Tara remains one of Hindi cinema's most memorable supporting performances. "She was one of the first people I spoke to. I didn't have any other name in my mind when I was writing Tara," Akhtar said.

At the reunion, the team also revisited the film's pivotal slap scene. Akshaye Khanna slapped Aamir Khan 17 times during the tense interval sequence, with Khan insisting on real contact for authenticity. By the time the scene wrapped, Khan's face was visibly swollen on one side.

What 25 Years Built

To mark the milestone, Akhtar and his producing partner Ritesh Sidhwani announced Excel Origins, a new initiative aimed at discovering, developing, and backing young filmmakers. "25 years ago, we started Excel Entertainment and began work on a film called Dil Chahta Hai. We had a simple brief — new voices and different ways of telling stories will find an audience," their statement read.

For the diaspora, 'Dil Chahta Hai' holds a particular place. It was among the first Hindi films that NRI audiences didn't have to explain or contextualize for non-Indian friends. Its portrayal of friendships that survived distance, different life stages, and the quiet drift of growing up resonated with a generation navigating identity across continents. Twenty-five years later, the film that nobody wanted to make remains the one everybody remembers.
